name: Colin Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to companies, unions, parties or government, and what you tell me is confidential. What's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage a 60-hectare apple and pear orchard for the Whitaker family. Winter is pruning, every tree by hand, which takes three of us about four months. Spring I'm up at night watching for frost on the blossom. Then thinning, spraying, and the picking season in September and October, when we've got thirty pickers on ladders and platforms.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Pruning, believe it or not. It's quiet, and every cut decides what that tree does for the next three years. Old Mr Whitaker taught me, and he'd walk behind me and say 'too much' or 'not enough' without even looking. Now I'm the one walking behind the young ones.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Frost and money. One cold night in April can take half the crop, and you can't do a thing. The pay's modest. My wife Ruth works part-time on reception at the doctor's surgery in town and sings in the church choir. We married last year, and between the wedding and the car, we've less than a month put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful, in its place. I use one of those AI apps now and then to check the frost forecast against what the weather station says, or to write up the spray records. Wouldn't post about it, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's no different from now. The apples grow at their own speed. What matters to me is the price the packhouse pays, and the weather in April.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Maybe let it do more of the spray records, which take me two evenings a month. Ask Mr Whitaker's son, who runs the business side now, for a rise after a good harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing here changes my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you start using the AI app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin showed me at Christmas. I watched him use it for a few months first, to see if it was any good. Then I tried it on the spray records, and it saved me an evening. That's about as far as I've gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Choir practice with Ruth, probably. She's been asking me to join the basses for a year. I keep saying the trees need me. They'd survive one evening.

S0.say: I'd say it's useful in its place. I use an AI app now and then to check frost forecasts and write spray records, but I wouldn't post about it.
S0.think: It's no different from now. Apples grow at their own speed, and what matters is the packhouse price and the April weather.
S0.do: Hands more of the spray records to the AI app to save an evening a month. Asks the owner's son for a rise after a good harvest.
S0.feel: Calm; nothing in his life changes.
S0.quote: She's been asking me to join the basses for a year. I keep saying the trees need me. They'd survive one evening.
S0.fieldNote: Colin is gentle, steady and family-centred, and he took up AI only after watching his cousin use it for months. The orchard sets the pace of his life. The choir story was a nice glimpse of his marriage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should keep the old way of learning, master and apprentice. You can't learn pruning from a screen. I'd say that at the growers' meeting, and they'd all nod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry about it a bit. If companies hire fewer beginners, the young lads I'm training might not get proper jobs elsewhere, and we'd lose them. There aren't many young people who want orchard work as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the Whitakers to keep taking on one apprentice a year, even if it costs. I'd use the AI for more of the paperwork once the other growers had shown it worked. And I'd start writing down what Mr Whitaker taught me, so it doesn't die with him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, slightly uneasy for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Writing down what Mr Whitaker taught you. What would be in it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which trees fruit better if you leave the old wood, which side of the orchard gets frost first, how to tell a pear's ready by the colour round the stalk. He's 84. Some of it's only in his head and mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you write it on paper, or let a computer help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paper first. Then maybe I'd ask the app to type it up neatly. Ruth says I write like a doctor, which is funny since she works for one.

S1.say: I'd say we should keep the master and apprentice way of learning, because you can't learn pruning from a screen. I'd say it at the growers' meeting.
S1.think: I worry a bit that fewer beginner jobs elsewhere mean we'd lose the young people I'm training. Few young people want orchard work already.
S1.do: Asks the owners to keep taking one apprentice a year. Uses AI for more paperwork once other growers show it works, and writes down the old owner's knowledge before it is lost.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, slightly uneasy for young workers.
S1.quote: He's 84. Some of it's only in his head and mine.
S1.fieldNote: His instinct is to protect knowledge passed between generations, which fits his traditional outlook. He's happy to use AI as a typist but not as a teacher. Mr Whitaker clearly means a great deal to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's hard on the office workers, and families and churches should help each other through it. I don't think the government should just hand out money. I'd say people should look at practical work, like orchards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, Ruth's job worries me. A doctor's reception is phone calls and bookings, and that's exactly what these assistants would do. If her hours go, we're down a third of our money, and we've only just married.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ruth to think about training as a healthcare assistant, hands-on work at the surgery, and see if they'd pay for it. I'd ask for extra hours in winter pruning for other growers nearby. And we'd put off thinking about children for a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for me, for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting off children. Is that something you've talked about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not properly. Ruth wants to start soon, and so do I. I'd hate for a computer in a doctor's office to decide when we have a family. Saying that out loud, it sounds daft. But it's true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said families and churches should help each other. What would that look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The church already does a food bank on Thursdays. If people lost jobs, I'd give a day a week of fruit, the seconds, the ones too ugly for the supermarket. Mr Whitaker would agree, I think.

S2.say: I'd say it's hard on office workers, and families and churches should help each other through it rather than relying on government handouts. People should look at practical work like orchards.
S2.think: Ruth's reception job is exactly what these assistants would do. If her hours go, we lose a third of our money just after getting married.
S2.do: Encourages his wife to train as a healthcare assistant at the surgery, ideally paid for by them. Takes extra winter pruning work for nearby growers and postpones starting a family for a year or two.
S2.feel: Anxious, not for himself but for their household.
S2.quote: I'd hate for a computer in a doctor's office to decide when we have a family.
S2.fieldNote: The threat reaches him through his wife's job, and the cost shows up as delaying children, which clearly hurt to say. His answer to hardship is church and community, not government. He'd give away second-grade fruit at the food bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the winners should do right by their communities, and the politicians should calm down and stop fighting. I'd say thank goodness there's still work for people who use their hands. I'd say it at the growers' meeting and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the orchard's safe for now. But house prices booming worries me, because Ruth and I rent a cottage in the village, and the owner's already hinted he'd sell if prices went up. And rich people buying land might buy orchards just to look at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the Whitakers whether there's a way to rent the old foreman's house on the orchard. I'd save every penny of overtime. And I'd keep an eye on whether any of the new money wants pick-your-own or orchard weddings, because I've seen other farms do well with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit unsettled. The job's fine. The home isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Orchard weddings. Would you really do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it kept the orchard going, yes. I'd want it done properly, not a circus. I've seen one farm do it well, near Ruth's parents. Blossom in May, long tables between the trees. Pays better than the apples, they say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the cottage owner did sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd move in with Ruth's parents for a while, which is a forty-minute drive from the orchard. I'd do it, but it'd mean leaving at five every morning in frost season. Ruth's mum would feed us well, at least.

S3.say: I'd say the winners should do right by their communities and the politicians should stop fighting. Thank goodness there's still work for people who use their hands.
S3.think: The orchard is safe for now, but our landlord has hinted he'd sell the cottage if prices rose. Rich buyers might also buy orchards just to look at.
S3.do: Asks the owners about renting the old foreman's house on the orchard and saves all his overtime. Watches whether new money creates demand for pick-your-own or orchard weddings.
S3.feel: Anxious and unsettled: the job is fine but the home is not.
S3.quote: Blossom in May, long tables between the trees. Pays better than the apples, they say.
S3.fieldNote: His home, not his job, is what's at risk here. He's open to orchard weddings once he has seen another farm do it well, which is classic steady adoption. Moving in with his in-laws is the fallback, and he faces it with good humour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robot pickers on apple trees aren't new. People have been testing them for years. I'd say they'd better be proven before anyone trusts them with a crop worth a year's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think picking will go first. Thirty pickers for two months is our biggest cost. Then maybe thinning and spraying. Pruning, I'd like to think, is too skilled, but I said that about picking ten years ago. I'm the best pruner in the county. I'd hate to find out that doesn't matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go and see the robots on someone else's orchard, a full season, before saying a word to the Whitakers. Then I'd offer to run them and keep doing the pruning myself. I'd learn the basics of the machines, the way I learned the AI app, slowly, once I'd seen it work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like a frost night in April that doesn't end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like a frost night that doesn't end. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a frost night, you stand in the orchard at three in the morning with the fans going, hoping. You can't stop it, you just watch. That's what this would feel like, but for years instead of one night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the apprentice you're training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn the robots as well as the trees. Both. I'd tell him the trees will still need someone who loves them. I'd believe it, mostly.

S4.say: I'd say robot apple pickers have been tested for years, and they'd better be proven before anyone trusts them with a year's crop.
S4.think: I think picking goes first, then thinning and spraying. I'd like to think pruning is too skilled, but I said that about picking ten years ago.
S4.do: Watches robots on another orchard for a full season before raising it with the owners. Then offers to run them while keeping the pruning, learning the machines slowly once proven.
S4.feel: Alarmed, like a frost night that goes on for years.
S4.quote: I'm the best pruner in the county. I'd hate to find out that doesn't matter.
S4.fieldNote: This is where his pride in a rare skill meets the fear that it won't count. He stays steady in method, a full season of watching first, even under threat. The frost night image was the most striking thing he said.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, because orchards are on the list and pickers go first. What would help is apprenticeships that keep the old skills alive alongside the new, and some sort of guarantee that skilled workers get first chance at running the machines. Not a handout. A fair shot.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask what we'd lose. An orchard is a hundred years of decisions by people who loved it. A robot can pick an apple. I'm not sure it can plant a tree for a grandson.

headlineQuote: I'm the best pruner in the county. I'd hate to find out that doesn't matter.
portrait: Colin Fischer is 27 and manages a 60-hectare apple and pear orchard for the Whitaker family, newly married to Ruth, who works on reception at the doctor's surgery and sings in the church choir. He's gentle, careful and proud of his pruning, taught by the 84-year-old Mr Whitaker, and he only takes up new tools after watching others use them for months. In the middle scenarios his fears run through Ruth's job and their rented cottage, and he would even put off having children. Robots that pick apples alarm him most, and he wonders if being the best pruner in the county will still matter. He looks to church, family and apprenticeships, not government, for help.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because orchards are a target and picking would be the first job to go.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships that keep old skills alive alongside new ones, and a guarantee that skilled workers get first chance at running the machines.
